title: Beige Book — October 15, 2025
html:
Official report: Summary · Full PDF Local PDF: 2025-10-15 Beige Book.pdf

Overall economic activity

"Economic activity changed little on balance since the previous report." Three Districts (Boston, Philadelphia, Richmond) reported slight to modest growth, five no change, and four (New York, Minneapolis, Kansas City, San Francisco) slight softening. Manufacturing faced difficult conditions from tariffs and softer demand. Lower interest rates helped some business lending and commercial construction, notably in Cleveland. Commercial real estate was mostly flat, energy generally down and agriculture generally weaker. Outlooks varied; one District warned a prolonged government shutdown could weigh on growth. The report was prepared by the San Francisco Fed.

Consumer spending

Retail spending edged down, though auto sales rose in some Districts as buyers pulled forward EV purchases before a federal tax credit expired at the end of September. International travel demand fell further; domestic demand was largely flat. Higher-income households kept spending on luxury travel, while lower- and middle-income households sought discounts amid rising prices and uncertainty.

Labor markets

Employment was largely stable, but labor demand was soft. More employers cut headcount through layoffs and attrition, citing weaker demand, uncertainty and in some cases "increased investment in artificial intelligence technologies." Hiring firms often preferred temporary or part-time workers. Labor supply was strained in hospitality, agriculture, construction and manufacturing, linked to immigration policy changes. Wages rose modestly to moderately; large health insurance premium increases lifted labor costs.

Prices

Prices rose further. Input costs grew faster, driven by import costs and services such as insurance, health care and technology. Tariff pass-through varied: some firms absorbed costs to protect market share, while some manufacturers and retailers passed on the full cost. Weaker demand lowered some material prices (steel in the Sixth District, lumber in the Twelfth).

Notable themes

  • K-shaped consumer: Affluent spending strong; others hunting for deals.
  • AI: Cited as one reason for headcount reductions.
  • Tariffs and immigration: Raising costs and straining labor supply.
  • Policy events: EV tax credit expiration; government shutdown risk; Minneapolis concern about China ending soybean purchases.

District highlights

  • Boston: Slight expansion, but mostly downside risks.
  • Cleveland: Commercial construction and financial services up on lower rates.
  • St. Louis: "Inflation is eroding consumer purchasing power"; agriculture strained and worsening.
  • Kansas City: Consumer loan portfolios weakened moderately; optimism for 2026, but 2026 price growth expected above 2025.
  • Dallas: Outlook worsened; inflation a top business concern.

Read-through for SPY

  • Flat growth with a split consumer favors companies serving higher-income households over mass-market retail.
  • Lower rates were starting to help lending and construction, a modest positive for cyclicals and financials.
  • Rising layoffs/attrition and AI-linked headcount cuts point to a softening labor market—supportive of further Fed easing but a risk to spending.
